notes:
I found useful material for most verses. Verses 6–7 and 13–18 are thin, and I couldn't find anything for the Lutheran or Pentecostal traditions as such, or on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or oca.org. Those gaps are listed at the end.

---

**v. 1**
- **Author's two titles.** Guzik says the order matters: Peter calls himself a bondservant first and an apostle second. The faith his readers "obtained" came by God's righteousness, not by human effort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **"Like precious faith."** Guzik quotes Clarke: Gentile believers were given the same faith and salvation as Jewish believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Jesus called God.** Guzik argues the Greek grammar shows Peter calling Jesus Christ both God and Savior. He backs this with Wuest and Blum. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Righteousness counted to believers.** Precept Austin reads the verse as saying believers share equally in salvation because God's righteousness is credited (imputed) to them. It adds that God also gives the faith itself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_11-11
- **Authorship.** Guzik notes that some deny Peter wrote this letter because its style differs from 1 Peter. He answers that the two letters had different purposes: 1 Peter encouraged believers facing persecution, while 2 Peter warns against false teachers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/

**v. 2**
- Grace and peace come "in the knowledge of God and Jesus our Lord." As we come to know God, we receive what we need for salvation and for daily living. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/

**v. 3**
- **What "knowledge" means.** Guzik, following Blum, says the Greek word means exact and thorough knowledge, not passing acquaintance. It is known by experience, not just by intellect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **How we gain it.** We come to know God through His Word, prayer and the community of His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **A personal relationship.** A Ligonier devotional says "knowledge" here mainly means an intimate relationship. So only those in a saving relationship with Christ have everything needed for life and godliness. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-divine-power
- **Nothing to add.** Precept Austin suggests the false teachers may have offered a "special doctrine." Peter's answer is that the Christian, like a newborn baby, already has all the equipment needed and only has to grow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_13-4

**v. 4 (a verse where traditions differ)**
- **Traditional reading.** Guzik says God's promises rest on His glory and virtue, so they are completely reliable. He compares sharing the divine nature to Paul's teaching on adoption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Not becoming God (Baptist).** Precept Austin, quoting MacArthur and others, says sharing the divine nature does not make believers God or "gods." The essence of God cannot be shared by a creature. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59754/
- **A growing share in God's life (Baptist).** Maclaren (quoted on Bible Hub) says the phrase means more than enjoying God's blessings: God Himself comes into us. He stresses *becoming* rather than *being*: the Christian lives by drawing life from God continually, and that share should grow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_peter/1-4.htm
- **Reformed.** A Ligonier devotional admits the exact meaning is "a bit unclear." It ties the phrase to the image of God: damaged in the fall, not lost, and being restored as we grow in holiness. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-divine-power
- **Calvin.** Monergism notes that Calvin, on this verse, called the gospel's goal "to deify us." For Calvin this meant sharing God's immortality and glory as far as human capacity allows. https://www.monergism.com/theosis
- **Orthodox "theosis," described by others.** I found no Orthodox source of its own. A Themelios article on The Gospel Coalition calls the phrase central to the Orthodox teaching of deification, but points out it sits in a passage about sanctification. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/salvation-as-theosis-the-teaching-of-eastern-orthodoxy/
- **GotQuestions.** No human being can ever become truly divine. "Partakers" means sharers or companions in God's nature through salvation, sanctification and sonship. https://www.gotquestions.org/theosis.html
- **Catholic.** Catholic Answers says no verse means human nature can be changed into God's nature. These verses mean human nature can share in it, and man always remains finite. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/can-man-become-god

**v. 5**
- **Effort is required.** Guzik says growth doesn't just happen. Believers work in partnership with God to "add" these qualities, and love is the capstone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **"Supply" doesn't mean supply faith.** Precept Austin, citing Hiebert, says readers are not asked to supply faith; they already have it. Paul Apple's summary: we work hard because we have been saved, not in order to be saved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59755/

**vv. 6–7**
- On self-control, Guzik reports Wuest's note that the Greeks used the word for someone not ruled by sexual desire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- The list shows God wants a well-rounded Christian life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- Precept Austin (quoting an older expositor) says reverence is the root idea of godliness. Love is the fullest expression of spiritual strength: a settled principle, not just an emotion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_15-7

**vv. 8–9**
- **Nearsightedness.** Guzik says lacking these qualities shows "eye trouble": seeing ourselves but not God. Quoting Morgan, such a person sees the things of time but not eternity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Forgetting the cleansing.** Guzik suggests this person may have forgotten how bad he was, what his cleansing cost, or how complete it is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/

**v. 10 (the main Calvinist–Arminian divide)**
- **Reformed and Baptist: confirming assurance, not salvation.**
  - Precept Austin distinguishes *security* (an objective fact: salvation is forever) from *assurance* (our own confidence). It says Peter is not teaching that a genuine believer can lose salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_110-11
  - It quotes Grudem: assurance can grow over the years as believers grow in these qualities. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_110-11
  - MacArthur, as quoted there, reads "never stumble" as never falling into doubt or despair about your spiritual condition. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_110-11
- **Gill (Baptist).** Calling and election can't be made surer in themselves or before God, because they rest on God's unchangeable purpose. They are made sure in the believer's own experience and before others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_peter/1-10.htm
- **Calvin.** Peter's point is that hypocrites have nothing solid in them. Those who prove their calling by good works are free from the danger of falling, because God's grace upholds them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/1-10.html
- **Spurgeon.** Quoted by Guzik, he explains why calling comes before election: we can know our calling first, and that shows our election. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Ligonier.** Practising the qualities of vv. 5–7 means we will not fall away. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/make-your-election-sure
- **Methodist and Wesleyan.**
  - Wesley reads "wherefore" against the background of the apostates of chapter 2. He urges readers not to throw away their calling and election. If they are diligent, they "shall never *finally* fall." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/2-peter-1.html
  - Clarke (Methodist): believers who are diligent won't stumble as the Jews did and lost their election. Those who don't do these things will fall, so election is not "absolute and unconditional." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/2-peter/1-10.html
- **Catholic translation note.** The Douay-Rheims and Catholic Public Domain Version add "by good works" ("that by good works you may make sure your calling"). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/2-peter/1-10.html

**v. 11**
- **An abundant entrance.** Guzik quotes F.B. Meyer: a ship can limp into port waterlogged or sail in with every sail set. Meyer also pictures a conqueror welcomed with singers. Guzik contrasts this with being saved "as through fire" (1 Cor 3:15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- **Wesley.** God calls us by His glorious power, toward eternal glory as the goal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_peter/1.htm

**v. 12**
- Because eternal destiny is at stake, the basics are worth repeating, as sports teams drill the fundamentals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-1/
- Precept Austin says Peter isn't apologising for repeating himself; he knows we are all forgetful. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_112-21

**vv. 13–14**
- "Earthly dwelling" (the "tent") is a figure for staying alive. Wuest (quoted) says Peter planned to stir up their minds by reminding them of truths they had already learned. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_112-21

**v. 19**
- **Is Scripture "more sure" than experience?** Precept Austin, following Vincent, reads the Greek word order as ranking Scripture above even the Transfiguration experience. It notes that A.T. Robertson prefers the other reading: the vision made the prophetic word more certain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_119-21
- **What "the prophetic word" covers.** It means the whole Old Testament, not just the books of the prophets. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_119-21

**vv. 20–21**
- **About where prophecy comes from.** Bible Hub's study notes say the verse is about the origin of prophecy: God, not human insight or invention. The stress is on Scripture's divine inspiration and authority. https://biblehub.com/study/2_peter/1-20.htm
- **How translations divide.** Some speak of the prophet's own understanding (NLT, NET: "the prophet's own imagination"). Others speak of the reader's interpretation (CEV: no one alone can understand the prophecies; Complete Jewish Bible: not to be interpreted by an individual on his own). https://biblehub.com/2_peter/1-20.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/2-peter/1-20.html
- **Supports Vincent's reading of v. 19.** Precept Austin says vv. 20–21 back Vincent's reading, because Peter grounds Scripture's reliability in its divine inspiration. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_119-21

---

**What I couldn't find (left out):**
- Commentary on vv. 15–18 (the Transfiguration). Guzik's page cut off after v. 12, and I didn't get Precept Austin's vv. 15–18 page.
- Ellicott, Gill or Pulpit on vv. 1 and 20–21.
- The netbible.org notes and bibleodyssey.org on authorship.
- Catholic or Orthodox teaching on "private interpretation" (v. 20).
- Any oca.org source on theosis.
- Lutheran and Pentecostal views.
- Any of these sites addressing prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

A follow-up session could start with biblehub.com/commentaries/2_peter/1-20.htm and the Precept Austin page for vv. 15–18.
